# Internal error when a ParamSpec captures the signature of a function with `*args: *Ts`

mypy crashes with an internal error when a decorator-like class captures, with a `ParamSpec`, a function whose `*args` is annotated with an unpacked `TypeVarTuple`, and the captured signature is later used.

## Reproduction

`t.py`:

```python
from typing import Callable

class capture[**P, R]:
    def __init__(self, func: Callable[P, R]): ...
    def __call__(self, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> C[P, R]: ...

class C[**P, R]: ...

@capture
def print_args[*Ts](*args: *Ts) -> tuple[*Ts]: ...

reveal_type(print_args(2))

def test[*Us](*xs: *Us) -> None:
    reveal_type(print_args(2, *xs, 4))
```

```
python -m mypy --python-version 3.12 --no-incremental t.py
```

Actual output: mypy aborts on line 12 (the first `reveal_type`):

```
t.py:12: error: INTERNAL ERROR -- Please try using mypy master on GitHub:
...
```

## Expected

No crash. The two `reveal_type` calls report (together with the unrelated `Missing return statement [empty-body]` errors for the `...` bodies on lines 5 and 10):

```
t.py:12: note: Revealed type is "t.C[[Literal[2]?], tuple[Literal[2]?]]"
t.py:15: note: Revealed type is "t.C[[Literal[2]?, *args: *tuple[*Us, Literal[4]?]], tuple[Literal[2]?, *Us, Literal[4]?]]"
```

That is, when the captured parameters are specialised with the argument types of the call, the variadic `*args` is expanded and normalised the same way as it is for an ordinary callable: a fixed-length unpack becomes plain positional parameters (`[Literal[2]?]`), and a part that stays variadic remains as a single `*args: *tuple[...]` parameter after the positional prefix.

statement:
# Internal error for `*args: Unpack[tuple[int, T]]` when `T` is a constrained TypeVar

mypy crashes while checking the body of a function whose `*args` is annotated with an unpacked tuple type that contains a `TypeVar` with value restrictions (constraints).

## Reproduction

`t.py`:

```python
from typing import TypeVar, Unpack

T = TypeVar("T", int, str)

def foo(*args: Unpack[tuple[int, T]]) -> None:
    reveal_type(args)
```

```
python -m mypy --python-version 3.12 --no-incremental --show-traceback t.py
```

Actual output: an internal error, with a traceback ending in

```
  ...
IndexError: list index out of range

t.py: error: INTERNAL ERROR -- Please try using mypy master on GitHub:
```

## Expected

No crash. As with any function using a constrained `TypeVar`, the body is checked once for each value of `T`, and each check sees `args` as the tuple with `T` replaced by that value, so `reveal_type(args)` reports one note per value, in order:

```
t.py:6: note: Revealed type is "tuple[int, int]"
t.py:6: note: Revealed type is "tuple[int, str]"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
```

(In the test suite's fixture environment the same two notes read `tuple[builtins.int, builtins.int]` and `tuple[builtins.int, builtins.str]`.)

statement:
# Overload call with an `Any` argument evaluates to plain `Any` even when a precise fallback overload exists

When an argument that is, or contains, `Any` makes a call match several overloads whose return types differ, mypy gives up and infers `Any` for the whole call. A common pattern, especially in numeric libraries, is a specific overload plus a fallback overload taking `list[Any]`/similar with a return type that is nearly as precise. The result should then be that precise type, not a bare `Any`.

## Reproduction

`t.py`:

```python
from typing import overload, Any

@overload
def f(x: list[int]) -> list[tuple[int, ...]]: ...
@overload
def f(x: list[Any]) -> list[tuple[Any, ...]]: ...
def f(x): pass

a: Any
la: list[Any]
li: list[int]
ls: list[str]

reveal_type(f(a))
reveal_type(f(la))
reveal_type(f(li))
reveal_type(f(ls))
```

```
python -m mypy --python-version 3.12 --no-incremental t.py
```

Actual output:

```
t.py:14: note: Revealed type is "list[Any]"
t.py:15: note: Revealed type is "list[Any]"
t.py:16: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[int, ...]]"
t.py:17: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[Any, ...]]"
```

## Expected

For `f(a)` and `f(la)` both overloads match because of the `Any`, but their return types, `list[tuple[int, ...]]` and `list[tuple[Any, ...]]`, are equivalent (each is compatible with the other, differing only by `Any`). The call should evaluate to the return type of the overload that contains `Any`, here `list[tuple[Any, ...]]`, rather than collapsing to `list[Any]`:

```
t.py:14: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[Any, ...]]"
t.py:15: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[Any, ...]]"
t.py:16: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[int, ...]]"
t.py:17: note: Revealed type is "list[tuple[Any, ...]]"
```

More generally, when an `Any` argument causes ambiguity between matching overloads and the return types of the matches are equivalent to each other (each compatible with every other), the call evaluates to the one of them that contains `Any`. In all other cases behaviour is unchanged.

Calls that are not ambiguous because of `Any` (`f(li)`, `f(ls)`) keep their current results.

meta.subject: Find precise fallback for ambiguous Any overloads (#22060)
meta.commitMessage:
Find precise fallback for ambiguous Any overloads (#22060)

It is a common pattern (especially in numeric libraries) to have a
fallback overload that has a relatively precise return type (i.e. not
just `Any` or `list[Any]`). We should try to find and use that overload
if there is an ambiguity caused by an argument that contains `Any`.

This will likely cause some new errors, but this should limit the
fallout from https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/22011
